text:
American cities have undergone a fundamental transformation since 1980, characterized by accelerating gentrification and widening economic inequality [Source: ev-1]. Gentrification levels were at their lowest in the 1970s and increased every decade until 2010 [Source: ev-3]. The rate of gentrification doubled after 2000 compared to the 1990s, affecting nearly 20% of lower-income neighborhoods in major cities [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2]. In New York, 128 tracts gentrified, which was the highest raw total among cities reviewed [Source: ev-2].

Economic disparities have intensified significantly across metropolitan areas. By 2018–2021, Federal Reserve data tracking over 3,140 inequality series confirmed that inequality had reached record levels [Source: ev-1]. Several metros exhibit extreme patterns where income ratios reach 18:1 between top and bottom earners [Source: ev-1]. Specifically, Atlanta and Washington D.C. have a 95/20 ratio of 18:1 [Source: ev-1]. New York City leads with a Gini coefficient of 0.5469, compared to the national average of 0.40 in 2013 [Source: ev-1].

Housing affordability has deteriorated as costs outpaced wage growth. Since 2000, home prices increased 177% while median household income grew only 92% [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-4]. On an inflation-adjusted basis, incomes rose just 8.5%, whereas home prices rose more than 56% [Source: ev-4]. The national price-to-income ratio is approximately 4.6–4.7 [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-4]. In California cities such as Los Angeles, San Jose, Long Beach, San Francisco, and San Diego, ratios range from 9.6 to 12.2—more than double the national average [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-4]. Five of the six large U.S. cities with the highest price-to-income ratios are in California [Source: ev-4].

Demographic shifts have accompanied these economic changes. Gentrifying neighborhoods saw population increases (+6.5%) and became whiter (non-Hispanic white share increased by +4.3 percentage points), while poverty rates decreased by 0.7 percentage points [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2]. In contrast, lower-income areas that did not gentrify experienced slight population losses (-2.4%), an increase in minority concentration, and a rise in poverty of 6.7 percentage points [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2]. Displacement patterns vary by race; residents from historically Black gentrifying neighborhoods tend to move to poorer non-gentrifying areas, whereas residents from other gentrifying areas often move to wealthier ones [Source: ev-1]. Since 1980, nearly 80% of the country's under-45 population growth was concentrated in metro areas with over 1 million residents [Source: ev-1] [ev-4].
